title: The £200M Winter Fuel row that cost Labour 8pp
narrative_md:
**Rachel Reeves needed to close a £22 billion 'black hole.' Instead she opened one in Labour's poll numbers.**

On 29 July 2024, three weeks after Labour's landslide, the new Chancellor announced Winter Fuel Payments would be means-tested to Pension Credit recipients — stripping the £200-£300 benefit from around 10 million pensioners. Within ten weeks Labour's polling lead had collapsed by 8 points.

The policy was fiscally modest: roughly £1.5 billion in annual savings, a rounding error against the £105 billion debt interest bill. But the political design was disastrous. WFP had been universal since Gordon Brown introduced it in 1997, paid automatically without application. Restricting it to Pension Credit — a benefit with a notoriously low take-up rate of 63% — meant many of the poorest pensioners would lose it through administrative friction alone.

DWP was caught flat-footed. Pension Credit claims surged 152% in the eight weeks following the announcement, overwhelming processing teams and producing 16-week backlogs. Age UK estimated 2.5 million pensioners in poverty or just above the threshold would lose out. The charity, joined by the National Pensioners Convention, lodged a judicial review challenging the failure to carry out a proper equality impact assessment.

The backbench revolt was the worst of the parliament's opening months. 52 Labour MPs abstained on the September 2024 Commons vote; one resigned the whip. Rosie Duffield cited WFP specifically when she quit Labour days later. Focus groups in Red Wall seats showed pensioners — Labour's most reliable 2024 voting bloc over 65 — felt 'betrayed on day one.'

By March 2025 Reeves had partially reversed course, raising the Pension Credit threshold and launching a £7.4 million take-up campaign. But the damage was done: YouGov's Labour lead shrank from 16 points in July 2024 to 8 by October, and the party's net favourability among over-65s dropped 19 points.

The episode became a case study in 'symbolic fiscal savings' — where the optics of the cut exceed any real consolidation. State Pension uprating, which Labour maintained via the triple lock at 4.1% for 2025-26, cost roughly £7 billion — more than four WFP means-tests. But cutting one benefit while raising another reinforced the perception that Labour was picking on the easiest target.

Reeves reportedly told colleagues in late 2024 she would not do it the same way again. By then, the poll damage had hardened into brand damage.
